video_title: Why Smart Investors Make Crazy Decisions — Alex Edmans | Ideas Lab | Ep.54
gist: LBS professor Alex Edmans (The Madness of Markets) argues sentiment measurably moves prices (World Cup exits cut ~0.5% next day; Spotify song valence tracks stocks and inversely bonds) and that unconstrained individuals can out-endure career-constrained professionals in crash-prone premia like momentum, especially in neglected small caps. He offers tactics (round-number limit-order offsets, rolling losers, written counter-theses) and warns of a 'big market delusion' in AI hyperscalers, having cut his own AI/tech exposure 6-9 months ago.

themes.theme: Mood moves markets: sports & music sentiment

insights.claim: When a national team is knocked out of the World Cup, that country's stock market falls about 0.5% the next day even after controlling for world market moves, equivalent to over 10 billion pounds wiped off the UK market in a day.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Exogenous mood shocks produce measurable, tradeable one-day index moves.
insights.quote: when a country gets knocked out of the World Cup, the market falls significantly the next day. To put some numbers on it, it's about half a percent

insights.claim: After England's World Cup loss to Argentina this summer, the London market opened about 0.5% lower despite same-morning good economic news (strongest UK growth in about 13 months), and Yahoo Finance partly attributed the drop to the defeat.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: The sports-sentiment effect still shows up 20 years after publication, even overriding positive macro data.

insights.claim: Professionals are not immune to emotion at work; the soccer-result evidence shows traders' extraneous moods leak into pricing decisions.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Build process guards against mood rather than assuming professional detachment.
insights.quote: You are human and you are affected by emotions even when you're in your job.

insights.claim: During Brazil's 2014 7-1 home loss to Germany, Brazilian stocks rose as goals went in because markets expected the defeat to hurt left-wing president Dilma Rousseff's re-election chances, as she had tied her identity to the team and stadium spending.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Sentiment shocks can transmit through political-risk channels, flipping the expected sign.

insights.claim: Aggregate happiness (valence) of a country's top-100 Spotify streamed songs, measured by The Echo Nest algorithm on the music rather than lyrics, is significantly positively correlated with that country's stock returns.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Music-streaming mood is a usable, economy-wide sentiment proxy.

insights.claim: Music-based national mood is negatively correlated with government bond prices, consistent with optimistic investors rotating money out of safe assets like gilts into equities.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Sentiment drives cross-asset rotation, so mood signals can inform stock-bond relative positioning.

insights.claim: Studying the effects of mood (behavioral congruence, e.g. song choices) rather than its many unobservable causes lets researchers capture aggregate sentiment that individual drivers like arguments or sick kids cannot reveal.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Look for revealed-behavior data exhaust as sentiment indicators rather than modeling causes.

insights.claim: Individual amateurs may have greater potential to beat the market than professionals because they are free of benchmarks, quarterly evaluation, client redemptions and career risk.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Retail's edge is structural (time horizon, no career risk), not informational.
insights.quote: perhaps sometimes amateurs might be able to beat the market more easier than professionals

insights.claim: Most individuals wrongly believe their edge is knowledge (e.g. using AI personally, or being a doctor who understands a drug), but they trade against specialist analysts with management access, so informational edge is illusory.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Before investing, identify a real edge; domain familiarity is not one.
insights.quote: Before you think about investing in the first place, think about what your competitive edge is.

insights.claim: Edmans put much of his money into equities in early 2009 without needing to call the bottom because his 30-40 year horizon meant interim losses did not matter, which a client-facing professional could not afford.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: The 'endurance game' lets long-horizon capital buy crises professionals can't hold through.

insights.claim: Clare College, Cambridge issued roughly 10 million pounds of debt to buy equities in 2009; over ~10 years the debt cost grew to about 15 million while the equity investment grew to about 30 million.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Institutions with long-dated liabilities and no external clients can lever into crises profitably.

insights.claim: Momentum anomalies persist 33 years after discovery partly because fund managers, undiversified in their own careers, avoid strategies that crash rarely, even though diversified clients would benefit.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Career-risk-driven under-exploitation keeps crash-prone premia available to unconstrained capital.
insights.quote: you're just weirdly worried about that 1% of the time where if it crashes, you're going to be out of a job.

insights.claim: Whether specialists or generalists outperform depends on where expertise lies; specialism can be in a theme (e.g. corporate culture, intangibles, obscure news) applied across all sectors, not just an industry.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Evaluate managers on the coherence of their edge, not sector breadth.
insights.quote: specialism can be in theme, not just industry.

insights.claim: The Parnassus Workplace fund, investing in companies with great workplaces across sectors, was found by Morningstar to be the best performing large-cap fund over 1, 3, 5 and 10 years.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Corporate-culture factor is a cross-sector edge with evidence of outperformance.

insights.claim: In April 2025 a frost wiped out about a third of Turkey's hazelnut crop; Teranova Capital spotted Turkish-language coverage ignored by Western media, flew to Turkey, invested $20 million in the country's only listed hazelnut processor, which rose 40% once the shortage hit headlines.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Language barriers and 'dusty corners' create slow information diffusion that can be harvested.

insights.claim: Without a clearly defined specialism, a fund struggles to articulate its edge; even Warren Buffett, diversified across sectors, defines his edge as analyzing intangibles such as brands and moats.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Ask any manager to name the edge; vague answers signal no edge.

themes.theme: Benchmarking, active share and the equity premium

insights.claim: Benchmarking is fundamentally sound because an active manager charging around 75bp must beat a passive fund charging around 5bp, but it becomes harmful when managers hug benchmarks to protect careers.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Pay active fees only to managers who deviate from the benchmark with conviction.

insights.claim: Career-concerned managers may hold AI stocks even while believing in a bubble, to avoid being the one who missed the boom, which means delivering index exposure at active fees.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Benchmark-hugging can prop up bubbles and fails clients paying for active judgment.
insights.quote: I don't want to be the muppet who's still out of of AI and missing out on on this big boom.

insights.claim: Active share, invented by academics nearly 20 years ago, is generally correlated with outperformance, while closet indexers with low active share are effectively overcharging clients.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Use active share as a screen for conviction when selecting funds.

insights.claim: Active share should not become a target (Goodhart's law); investors should check whether a fund's active positions reflect its claimed expertise rather than trading for its own sake.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Pair active-share screens with a consistency check against stated edge.

insights.claim: Over the 10 years to December 2025, T-bills returned about 2% a year versus about 15% for the S&P 500, a 13% gap; over other periods the premium is around 7%, versus 3-4% that reasonable risk-aversion models justify (the equity premium puzzle).
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Equities structurally overcompensate for risk, favoring long-horizon equity holders.

insights.claim: A global active fund can legitimately add value by tilting to markets where the equity premium is unusually rich relative to risk, but only if clients could not replicate this cheaply via country index funds; outperformance from beta (e.g. beta 1.5) is not alpha.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Judge absolute-return claims on risk-adjusted alpha, not raw outperformance.

insights.claim: Momentum (buy 6-month winners, short 6-month losers) works because confirmation bias causes investors to underreact to news, and it holds globally across equities, bonds, currencies and nearly all asset classes, pointing to common human psychology.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Trend following has a durable behavioral foundation across asset classes.

insights.claim: Amazon launched what became AWS in 2006, but markets did not value it until AWS reported income separately in 2015, illustrating underreaction to information that conflicts with an established narrative.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Hidden segments inside narratively-pigeonholed companies can be mispriced for years.

insights.claim: Momentum crashes are partially predictable: a study by two professors who also work at AQR and Goldman Sachs found momentum typically underperforms when the VIX is high.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Scale down momentum exposure when implied volatility is elevated.
insights.quote: when VIX, which is the volatility index, is high, momentum is typically going to be underperforming.

insights.claim: A 'level two' strategy asks where a bias is most prevalent: momentum is stronger in small stocks with little analyst coverage because news about them goes unnoticed, while media focuses on the Magnificent 7 and large caps.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Apply behavioral signals where attention is scarcest for stronger effects.

insights.claim: Layered 'corner' momentum strategies (e.g. small caps with negative earnings) are not scalable for large institutions due to illiquidity and few names, making them better suited to sophisticated individuals or small funds.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Capacity constraints leave niche anomaly corners to small capital.

insights.claim: Because limit orders cluster at round numbers, prices often fail to reach them; Edmans places sell orders just below (e.g. 99.9 vs 100) and buy orders just above (e.g. 125.10 vs 125.00) to front-run the cluster and get filled.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Offset limit orders slightly inside round numbers to improve fill probability.
insights.quote: what I want to do is front run, I want to get in before other people get in or get out before other people get out.

insights.claim: The disposition effect (selling winners early, holding losers to break even) is doubly costly: momentum means losers tend to keep falling and winners keep rising, and selling winners crystallizes capital gains tax.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Overriding the urge to sell winners and hold losers improves both returns and taxes.

insights.claim: Rolling a losing position directly into a new stock (e.g. selling Tesco to buy Vodafone) mentally keeps the trade 'live' and helps investors realize losses, a fix supported by a research study.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: A practical behavioral hack to cut losers without admitting defeat.

insights.claim: Checking portfolios often leads to trading on already-priced news, buying high and selling low; infrequent checking (as Warren Buffett advises) shifts decisions to long-term factors.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Reduce monitoring frequency to avoid stale-news trading.

insights.claim: Investors should write down the case against each trade (e.g. AI fund P/E of 50 vs a norm near 30) and can use ChatGPT to generate counterarguments; written theses also enable post-mortems that separate bad theses from bad luck.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Written pre-mortems and kill criteria discipline both entries and post-trade evaluation.

insights.claim: Outsourcing 'ugly decisions' (exits, cuts) to someone else, such as a spouse, risk manager or CIO office, counters the reluctance to admit mistakes; Edmans applies this by choosing the most critical literary agent and asking reviewers to cut weak sections.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Institutionalize sell discipline with an independent party.

themes.theme: Big market delusion and AI hyperscalers

insights.claim: The 'big market delusion' occurs when excitement about a new technology lifts every company in the sector so that combined valuations imply an implausible industry size, violating an adding-up constraint since not all can win.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Sum sector valuations to test whether the implied total market is plausible.
insights.quote: Not every single company can become a winner. Not everybody can get gold medals.

insights.claim: In the early 2020s the combined valuation of EV makers such as Nio, Tesla and XPeng exceeded that of the entire traditional car market, before the sector turned south in 2022-2023.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: EVs are a recent template for how a big market delusion unwinds.

insights.claim: Applying the big market delusion to AI, not every hyperscaler will win and some may overinvest or invest in the wrong things, so the sector may be priced as if all are winners.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Be selective or underweight within AI rather than owning the whole basket.

insights.claim: Edmans reduced his AI and tech exposure about 6-9 months ago, locking in gains partly ahead of a large mortgage refinancing in about a year, accepting missed upside to avoid a bubble unwind.
insights.speaker: Alex Edmans
insights.so_what: Liability timing should drive de-risking of richly valued winners.
